subject: wendigo
pitch:
Category: Monster.
Subject: wendigo.
Style: folk horror.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a full module for a wendigo in folk horror style, aiming for a manageable length while staying accurate to the SDK API since I can't test it directly. I'm sketching the creature's design: a tall, emaciated humanoid around 2.6 meters with an elk or deer skull head, antlers, sunken glowing eyes, long clawed arms, and a visible ribcage.

Working out the skeleton structure and body proportions — hips rooted around 1.4m, spine chain up through chest and neck to head, with digitigrade-style legs and digit chains for fingers, plus folk horror details like frost, moss, bone talismans, and ritual daub paint. Now I'm setting up the imports and module scaffolding for the builder library.

On the glow effect, I'm weighing whether to import a documented kit helper or just write my own lightweight glow function to reduce risk — settling on writing a local helper that handles mesh parts and material emissive properties safely.

Now I'm sketching the palette for a folk horror aesthetic: desiccated grey-brown skin tones, bone and ash colors, rust-red for blood, frost white, and a sickly pale teal or ember glow for the eyes.

I'm settling on cold green-white glowing eyes contrasted with a dim orange ember glowing inside the ribcage, plus twine, straw, ochre red ritual markings, charcoal, and matted fur as supporting textures. I'm now planning the texture list, starting with an eye glow effect using a hollow socket with a glowing pupil-like decal.

Then I'm planning additional textures: matted fur tufts hanging along shoulders and limbs, torn rag strips for a loincloth with stitched edges, and a glowing ochre-red ritual rune symbol decaled onto the ribcage or skull, possibly tied to a spiral antler motif.

I'm also considering a straw hex-sign charm hanging from strings, frost/ice crystal cards, raven feathers fluttering from the antlers as a folk-horror nod to crows, moss and lichen patches on antlers and shoulders, and spiky teeth for the mouth. That gives roughly eight distinct textures to layer: eye glow, fur, tatters, sigil, hex charm, frost, feathers, and lichen.

Now I'm planning the paint shaders: mottled countershaded skin in grey-purple, grained bone with staining, gradient antler paint from dark brown base to pale tips, muddy gradient paint for the feet, plus fur, rope, and charcoal paints. Then I'm laying out the skeletal joint chain -- hips, spine, chest, neck, head -- positioning each point to create a stooped, forward-leaning posture.

For the head joint, I'll use `neck.at(1)` as the position reference, since ChainPoint should convert to a frame-like position, with the parent joint inferred automatically from that chain point.

For the torso, I'm planning a skeletal loft that's narrow and emaciated, with the spine forming a visible ridge down the back and ribs rendered as protruding arc-like sweeps around the chest, exposing a dark cavity beneath stretched skin.

Working out rib placement, I'm computing each rib as a curved path from spine to sternum, swept with a thin bone-colored radius and attached to the nearest spine joint, while making the ribs sit slightly outside the sunken chest loft so they read as visible bone under thin skin.

Now I'm setting loft stations along the spine with varying width and depth—narrower at the waist, flaring out at the pelvis, ribcage, and shoulders—and attaching the loft to the spine/hips bone chain, with the neck handled as a separate sweep along its own chain.

I'm also adding a pelvis box for leg attachment and placing the hip sockets slightly offset from center, setting up for the long digitigrade wendigo legs with their sunken knee joints.

For the legs, I'm working through a four-segment chain (thigh, shin, cannon, foot) using the sole constraint so the foot stays flat along the ground. Since the summed segment lengths exceed the hip height, the IK solver will need to bend the joints rather than stretch straight down to reach the toe target.

I need bends only at the two inner joints, with the knee going forward and the hock going back. The current lengths give a nearly straight leg, so I should lengthen the segments for a more pronounced digitigrade bend — making the hip taller but giving the wendigo's legs a leggier, more dramatic stance.

I want the knee bending forward and the hock pulling back, keeping the natural zigzag feel across the three segments. I'm setting up the chain call with five joint positions and matching names for hip, knee, hock, ankle, and toe, figuring out whether the toe counts as an extra tip joint beyond the four spans.

Passing the point array as a polyline, since a chain just needs one joint per span plus a tip — I'll rename the last joint "footL" to match the leg's anatomy. I'm also determining side naming by checking the root joint's X position, using "L" for positive X and "R" otherwise, and keeping hips as the parent for both legs.

For thickness I'm tapering the leg with a radius function along the chain — thick at the thigh, narrowing through the knee, shin, hock, cannon, down to the ankle — using smooth round caps at the foot end. Then for the foot itself, I'm planning three forward toes plus a dewclaw, each built as a separate swept polyline branching off the ankle point, with claws at the tips.

Writing toe capsules and claw spikes...

That checks out fine, so I won't over-engineer the foot attachment — I'll just use the chain's tip joint for the foot bone. For arms, I'm planning a T-pose-ish stance with shoulders extended laterally and drooping slightly, sketching out upper arm, forearm, and hand lengths with fingers.

Defining arm chain joints...

Still placing finger joints...

So the frame resolves with normal pointing up and binormal horizontal, giving rx as front-back width and ry as vertical thickness for the palm capsule. I'm tapering the arm radius from shoulder to wrist (0.06 to 0.03) and adding bone-spur spikes at the elbows pointing back-up for a gaunt, knobbly look rather than muscular definition.

Now I'm figuring out the shoulder and spine details — adding small spheres at the shoulders to suggest scapula bumps with bone showing through, and trying to work out how to place spikes along the back following the torso's loft path to suggest a vertebrae ridge, though I'm not fully certain how the loft path's angle parameter maps to the dorsal direction on a vertical sweep.

So angle 0 corresponds to the back, meaning the dorsal surface sits at the default angle along the sweep's tangent frame. I'll place vertebrae along the torso's spine using spikes at that dorsal position for each segment.

For the ribs and chest cavity, I'm sketching arcs that curve around the torso at a range of angles, generating catmull sweeps through points sampled from the torso surface to carve out rib shapes and a hollow inner chest for depth.

I'll place 7 rib pairs along the chest zone (t ≈ 0.38–0.8), each a sweep following the torso curve, plus a sternum sweep down the front center. Since the ribs are meant to look sunken and visible, I'll need the torso skin color to reflect that gaunt appearance.

For the belly, I want hip bones poking through — sharp iliac spikes jutting out near the pelvis front using stick geometry. Then for the head, I'm building an elk-like skull on a humanoid neck: a scaled sphere cranium, a tapered frustum-box muzzle extending forward, and a separate lower jaw bone connected at a joint, all painted in bone color.

Now I'm designing the jaw hinge at the back-lower skull, with the mandible made from two rods forming a V shape plus a chin, plus small cone teeth along the jaw edges and longer fang-like canines on top. For eye sockets, I'm making dark embedded spheres with a smaller glowing sphere inside to suggest sunken, eerie eyes, considering whether to add a textured plane for extra detail like a glowing ring or slit pupil.

I'll apply the eye texture as a decal directly onto the socket's spherical surface rather than a flat plane, since decals project onto the surface geometry and can still glow through emissive mapping with alpha transparency handling the background. I also need to orient the head joint to aim slightly forward-down, setting up local axes for forward, up, and right directions relative to the bone.

Using named local-direction words like forward, up, and left to position things on the head avoids confusing myself with raw axis signs, and I've confirmed from the decal example that left maps to positive X with mirroring tied to a side variable. Now I'm working out where to anchor the cranium center and skull proportions relative to the head joint, keeping the elk's skull narrower than a typical mammal.

I'll define a helper that builds absolute positions from a fixed head reference point, with parts bound to the head bone so I can skip local-space conversions, and set the head joint's direction with a slight downward tilt to keep orientation neutral.

Now I'm working out the skull as an ellipsoid and the snout as a tapered frustum box extending forward from the head center, and I need to pin down the frame convention — which axis maps to width versus height when the bone's forward direction runs along z with no explicit up vector.

With that convention set, I'm shaping the upper jaw as a tapered box narrowing toward the tip, adding a nose ridge, dark nostril boxes, and exposed palate teeth, plus a crest ridge along the skull top between the antlers. Then I'm setting up the jaw joint behind the cranium with its own pivot point and starting to build the mandible from paired rods.

Posing the jaw open about 12-14 degrees forward to show teeth, considering whether to add a dried, stringy tongue for extra folk-horror creepiness, and leaning toward a simple version if budget allows.

For teeth I'm planning six cone-shaped teeth per side along the upper and lower jaw edges, oriented downward on top and upward on the bottom, plus longer fangs near the muzzle front for extra menace. I'm keeping part counts within the 180-340 budget while considering whether to add any human-like features for unsettling contrast.

For the overall creature concept, I'm leaning into a wendigo-deer fusion—desiccated skin stretched over a deer skull, with dried remnants on the neck and a fur ruff. The antlers are the signature feature, so I'm sketching out a branching main beam using curved points sweeping up and back from the skull base to around 3.8m total height, though that height feels like it might be excessive and needs reconsidering.

Scaling things back to a 3.6m total height feels more workable for the stage while still nodding to wendigo lore's giant proportions, with antlers reaching up to 3.5m and a wide ±0.5 spread. Now I'm defining the tine-branching logic—computing root points and tangents along the main antler beam so smaller tines can emerge at specific points with their own curved sweeps.

Still writing tine geometry...

For coloring, I'm setting up a gradient that transitions the antler surface from a dark bone tone at the base to a pale tip color, blended with noise-based grain to avoid a flat, artificial look.

Now I'm thinking through adornments hanging off the antlers — lichen, feathers, twine with a hex charm, small crow skulls — and working out how to wrap twine around the beam using a closed sweep path rather than a full spiral, since that's simpler to get looking right.

Frames should convert fine into points for catmull, so I'll explicitly set bone: head on the sweeps so they attach to the nearest joint rather than defaulting. Now I'm sketching a buildAntler function that assembles the beam, tines, brow tine, wraps, lichen, and feathers for a given side, mirroring x by the side sign.

Writing beam point coordinates...

I'm placing the brow tine angling forward and slightly up near the base of the beam, then adding a second tine further along angled upward and forward, keeping the overall creature height around 3.8m even though it makes for a fairly tall figure.

Still defining tine positions...

Writing paint shader logic...

Finishing the skull paint function, then moving to body details — sweeping the neck geometry with skin tones and tendon lines, and adding a folk-horror collar of bone and teeth around the neck.

Still working out teeth placement...

For torso, I'm planning a sigil decal on the chest and tattered loincloth rags hanging from a hip loop, using `along` to space frames around that loop for attaching the hanging cards.

For the bone binding, I'm leaning toward anchoring the cards to the hips joint for rigidity, and figuring out the loop plane orientation by considering how the hips joint's default direction relates to world up when no explicit aim is set.

Now I'm worried the loop plane at the hips height might clip right at the loft's start point, causing a surface intersection failure, so I'm adjusting the loft to begin slightly below the hips so the plane cleanly crosses the surface rather than hitting the cap edge.

With that resolved, I'll use loop-based sweeps for the belt strap too, adding hanging charms and bone decorations, plus tattered rag cards hanging from the belt with varied sizes and bend for a worn look, and considering fur strips on the thighs and forearms along with a fur mane across the shoulders and back.

Now I'm scattering fur-textured cards across the upper back and shoulders, filtering hits by position and normal direction so they cluster on the back rather than the chest, with leaning and bending applied for a matted, layered mantle effect over the shoulders.

Checking the back curvature against the torso lean, I realize a flat extruded cape would intersect or hover oddly as the spine angles forward. Simpler to scatter pelt-strip cards hanging from a shoulder-level loop rather than sweeping a continuous surface.

I'm looping strips around the shoulder frame, filtering them to the back half so the cape drapes only behind the torso, and considering adding dangling hide strips from the forearms as flapping rags using a similar card-chain approach.

Since cards sharing a texture count as a single part for budget purposes, I can scatter plenty of fur cards cheaply on the shoulders. For glow effects, I'm planning glowing eyes via decal and a small ember sphere glowing inside the ribcage.

I'm also sketching frost crystal cards for the antlers and shoulders, pale cyan and non-glowing, and starting to spec the texture sheets—first the eye texture with a glowing radial disc and slit pupil inside a dark irregular socket ring, then moving on to the fur texture.

Defining more texture assets...

Skipping the bone charm idea. I'm thinking about how to hang the lichen, feathers, and hex charms from the antler beams using frames positioned along beam points, then moving on to the skin paint treatment: a grey-brown base with dark mottled patches, purple bruise tones, frost-dusted highlights on upper surfaces, and mud near the feet.

Writing skin shader code...

I need to keep the flat color palette under 64 colors, with darkness, bone, and antler paints defined separately from rope textures. For the torso decal, I'm figuring out how to position the sigil on the belly surface using a raycast against the torso geometry.

Now I'm tallying up the part count across the skeleton: torso, fourteen ribs, sternum, roughly eight vertebrae spikes, hips, and arm sweeps.

Fingers, thumbs, palms add about 25 parts; legs with toes contribute around 12-15 more; the head alone—skull, teeth, antlers with tines and wraps—could be 50 parts, plus charms and rags. I'm landing on roughly 230 parts total, which feels reasonable, so now I'm working out the leg IK, placing hip sockets and toe targets in local coordinates.

Measuring the hip-to-heel distance against the combined thigh, shin, and cannon lengths, I realize this is a three-segment chain rather than a simple two-bone setup, so I need the cannon to hang vertically beneath the hip while the thigh and shin form their own two-bone solve up to the cannon's top point.

A knee bent 0.38 forward is pretty pronounced — gives a tall, stalking stance, like a bird-legged creature with the hock sitting directly above the ankle rather than angled back like a dog's.

I'll settle on segment lengths [0.56, 0.56, 0.46, 0.24] to keep proportions sane, then add a small bony knee spike protruding forward at that joint for a monstrous detail. Setting up the leg chain with five points — hip, knee, hock, ankle, toe — connected across four spans with matching joint names.

Still defining leg radii...

For a faceted, woodcut-style aesthetic I'll lean toward fewer sides with smooth shading disabled on the limbs and antlers, giving them an angular, stylized look while the torso keeps smoother default shading. I'm also considering adding a gradient on the legs so they darken toward exposed bone near the ankles.

Now I'm mapping out the arm skeleton: shoulder socket near the torso edge, elbow bent outward and down, wrist further out and twisted, with the hand chain parented to the arm's tip joint and oriented outward along the bone direction.

Working out the finger geometry...

Still defining claw geometry...

Now I'm positioning the thumb separately, giving it a base point slightly behind and below the fingers, angled forward and outward since the palm faces down.

For the fingers and thumb, I'm naming each joint segment with a consistent regex-safe naming scheme and sweeping tapered chains with small radii and rounded caps, tagging them with a "digit" role, then anchoring the arm chains to the appropriate spine joint near the chest socket.

For the arm itself, I'm sweeping along the chain path with a skin color and hex cross-section, then building the palm as a tapered sweep between wrist and palm-end points with an elliptical radius profile and rounded caps, and adding a small spike at the elbow for a spur detail.

Now I'm adding a shoulder blob sphere bound to the first arm joint so it rotates with the shoulder, then starting an acromion-like spike protrusion on the torso near the shoulder point.

I'm also planning clavicle rods running from the sternum to the front of the shoulder for an exposed collarbone look, and sketching scapula plates as flattened boxes on the back to suggest shoulder blades.

Defining the spine curve and loft stations...

Mapping out seven rib stations along the torso's t parameter, spacing them to align with the ribcage region around y 1.8-2.2, then building each rib's curve from angled points with a slight lift and attaching them to the spine bone for weighting.

Mirroring ribs to the opposite side by negating the angle, tapering rib radius toward the spine end, and lifting them slightly above the torso skin so they poke through visibly like a starved figure.

For the sternum, I'm tracing a path along the torso surface and sweeping a thin profile to form the central bone. Then for the ember, since it'd be hidden inside the skin, I'm instead placing it bulging partially through a gap between the ribs near the chest front — like a glowing heart poking out — sized so it protrudes roughly half a sphere's worth through the rib cage.

Now I'm adding a jagged dark-red wound rim around the ember: a flattened disc of dark flesh plus a crater shape placed slightly lower and behind the glowing ember sphere, using a cylinder for the crater and a sphere embedded partway for the ember itself, then applying a glow material with an emissive clone.

My glow helper normalizes input into a mesh array, clones and caches each material by strength to avoid duplicating standard materials, setting emissive color, map, and intensity. Since materials are shared per color or texture across parts, this caching should keep things efficient, and part-returning functions like decal, stick, and cards all expose consistent mesh access for this. With that settled, I'm moving on to work out the head joint placement in detail.

Now I'm plotting the neck chain from chest to a head joint, then positioning the skull as an ellipsoid centered just above and ahead of the neck's end so the head tilts forward naturally, working out exact coordinates and radii so the neck geometry tucks into the base of the skull correctly.

Next I'm shaping the snout as a tapering frustum running forward with a slight downward tilt, adding small nostril spheres near the tip and a thin nasal ridge rod along the top for definition.

Then I'm placing the upper teeth row along both sides of the snout's underside, computing how the snout's bottom contour tapers from the base to the tip so the teeth sit flush against the curving jawline.

Positioning the cone's center accounting for height offset so the base sits into the jaw. Now thinking about fangs near z=1.05 as small curved tusks, thin and short, mimicking elk upper canines.

For the lower jaw, I'm defining the mandible joint pivot and aim point, then sweeping curved rods on each side for the jaw bone with a cross-chin bar connecting them, plus a flattened sphere at the ramus for the jaw angle bulge, and placing lower teeth along the mandible curve.

For the jaw hinge I'm using a 14° rotation around the X-axis to tip the lower jaw forward, with teeth and rods bound to that bone. Now I'm placing the eye sockets as dark deep-set spheres near the cranium front, adding a brow ridge capsule above each, and planning a glowing eye decal facing forward on the socket surface.

I'm checking that the eye socket sphere actually protrudes slightly past the skull's ellipsoid surface at that position, creating a natural dark-blob-under-brow-ridge look rather than sinking entirely inside the bone.

To give it a more recessed appearance, I'm adding a small bone-colored torus as a rim around the socket, oriented outward along the same axis as the eye decal, so the eye looks set within a ridge rather than floating on a bump.

Now I'm thinking about ears — elongated, tattered leaf shapes like elk ears, positioned near the top of the head and extruded outward and slightly back, defining a tapered outline for the leaf silhouette.

Working out the perpendicular axis vectors for the tilted ear orientation on both sides, keeping the dot products at zero for proper alignment. For the skull texture, I'll keep it simple with fur on the ears rather than adding separate dried-skin patches.

For hair, I'm setting up a neck ruff using a ring of fur cards around the neck that face outward and lean downward along a flow direction, so they stick out then droop like matted strands. Now moving on to the eyes.

Then I'm draping long matted hair cards from the skull back down behind the neck, placing frames at the cranium facing upward with a steep lean angle so strands hang downward, using seven strands and reusing the FUR texture for the look. I'm also setting up a helper function to hang decorative cards like antlers from arbitrary points, with frames facing up and configurable size and flow direction.

I decide to add twine wrapping around the antlers plus a small hex charm hanging from a tine using its own string texture, but I'll skip adding a perched crow or other skull charms to keep the line count manageable—maybe just a few scattered feathers instead.

For the wrist and ankle cuffs, I'm designing a wrap helper that generates a ring of points around a bone's tangent direction, then sweeps a closed Catmull-Rom curve through them to form a thin cuff shape with no end caps needed since the path loops.

I'm using chain.nearestJoint to attach rigid bones to each wrap point for the arms, and planning similar twine and bone bracelets for the ankles. For the belt, I'm sweeping a thin loop and adding hanging tooth and bone charms as cone-shaped parts suspended along the loop.

For the hip loop placement, I'm checking that the plane orientation follows the joint's upward bone axis so the cross-section sits correctly at the waist height.

The belt itself I'll sweep along that loop with a fixed twine color and rigid attachment to the hips bone. For the rags, I'll sample points directly off the loop by index rather than relying on tangent callbacks, framing each sampled point with an upward vector to keep things simple and predictable.

Front rags should hang longer than back ones, so I'll vary the strip length based on how close the sample angle is to the front-facing direction.

For the back cape, I'm thinking about looping at the spine3 joint position to get a tilted chest cross-section plane, letting strips hang from the upper back near the shoulders rather than lower down.

I'll use a literal point with a direction vector instead of a bone-anchored frame, filtering so strips only originate from the back half of the torso by checking z position against the spine's center depth, excluding arms. I need to watch for the plane intersecting the shoulder cap region near the top of the torso.

For fur, I'm scattering with a minimum distance and filtering by height and normal direction to keep it on the upper back and shoulders, with cards leaning backward to flow naturally along the surface. I'm also considering adding a few frost-touched strands along the shoulder tops and antler beams, plus darkening the interior of the mouth where the snout meets the jaw.

Adding dark palate box...

Now I'm shaping a hanging tongue as a curved sweep from the jaw outward, using a reddish color and a drooping curve of points extending past the jaw line to make it look like it's dangling.

I'm adding small burr spheres at the antler bases in dark bone tone to anchor the pedicles, then considering decorative forehead marks — thinking of a small ochre glyph or tally-stroke decal on the cranium, possibly reusing the existing sigil texture.

Counting textures so far (eye, fur, tatters, sigil, hex, frost, feather, lichen), I'm weighing a ninth: a handprint decal, a simplified ochre palm with four fingers and thumb, placed on the snout sides or ribs as a tribal marking.

Decal placement needs target surfaces — I'll apply it on the torso. Now I'm checking floor contact for the toe claws, making sure the claw tips stay just above y=0 by computing the drop vector from the toe tip along the claw direction, confirming the final height is small but positive.

For the foot, I'm defining the toe geometry as capsules branching from the sole target point, spreading forward with slightly varying base and tip radii so the claws taper naturally near the ground, plus adding a small rear spur toe for structure.

I'm verifying the heel-to-toe direction of the IK foot segment points correctly along +Z, and planning to add low-opacity mud texture near the feet. Then I'm moving on to bone binding — attaching toes to the foot bone under the ankle joint — before starting the pelvis structure with bone-colored iliac crest wings extending from the hips.

Now I'm placing the hip joint spheres and deciding against a tail for the wendigo rig. For the spine, I'm sweeping a series of dorsal spikes along the torso's back curve, adjusting their radius and taper so they ride naturally along the hump from the upper to lower back.

Including hanging items sized [0.07,0.35]. Now I'm writing the SVG markup for the eye, using a radial gradient for a glowing teal-white core...

Writing SVG code...

Still writing SVG code...

I also need to work out orientation: the drawing's bottom edge is the root attachment point, so when the card hangs downstream, it actually appears upside-down -- the ragged tip edge ends up at the top of the frame, with the root edge visible at the bottom of the viewer's perspective.

The same logic applies to the hex charm: since its tip points downward with the string at the top of the drawing's own coordinate space, viewing it rotated 180° means I should draw the string attachment at the bottom of the viewBox and the charm's tip at the top, so that once rotated, the string appears correctly at the top.

For the other hanging elements — feather, lichen, fur, and tattered edges — I'm using the same orientation convention: root or attachment point at the bottom of the file coordinates (y near 64/80), with the free tips, strands, or ragged edges extending upward toward y=0, since these will be viewed in their natural orientation without rotation.

Now I'm working through card geometry for the hanging cards with the lean and flow settings — thinking about how the face orientation and viewing direction (from downstream looking back) affects whether the drawing appears rotated 180° versus mirrored, and confirming that a 180° rotation (not a vertical flip) is what produces the "upside down but not mirrored" result that's intended.

For the hex charm design, I'm laying out the SVG structure so that when flipped for hanging, the tassel strands end up correctly dangling below the ring and the attachment string sits at the top. Writing SVG code...

Still writing antler glyph paths... I'm planning to layer a dark outline stroke beneath the ochre lines to give the sigil depth, probably by defining the path data once as a constant and rendering it twice. Now moving on to sketching the handprint icon with a rounded palm shape and four fingers.

Still writing feather details... I'm also sketching the lichen moss strands with wavy green-toned paths, then moving on to set up the gradient helper strings before starting the main TypeScript module imports and utility functions.

Defining color palette constants...

Still defining the spine chain... I'm noticing the first spine joint lands exactly on the hips joint, giving that bone zero length, so I'm weighing whether to nudge the spine chain's starting point upward instead.

Settling on hips at (0, 1.38, -0.1) and starting the spine chain just above it at (0, 1.45, -0.08) so there's a small, real bone length between them. Now I'm sketching the neck chain as a Catmull-Rom path parented to the top spine joint, with two intermediate neck joints.

Then I'm placing the head joint parented to the second neck joint, pointed forward and slightly down, followed by the jaw joint parented to the head. I'm also sketching the torso loft call, binding it to both the spine and hips as its driving bones.

Checking the loft and sweep parameters now — confirming section shape, sides count, and smoothness settings for the neck sweep look consistent with the docs.

Shifting to the pelvis and leg sockets, I'm satisfied the torso width and socket sphere placements line up fine, and card weights inherit correctly from body bones.

Now starting the antler builder function...

Writing tine geometry function...

I'm sizing the wrap rings so they taper with the beam radius, then placing lichen clusters, feathers, and a hex charm at specific points along the beam for decoration.

Hanging cards dangle from points on the beam while frost cards stand upright facing all directions with cross visibility. To keep the code concise, I want to gather lichen, feather, and charm frames into shared arrays so I can call the card-generating function once per texture across both antlers instead of duplicating logic.

Setting up the module imports now, trimming unused helpers like polyline, offset, and DEG since I'll handle vector math directly with THREE.Vector3.

Defining the skin paint function next, layering noise-based color mixes for mottled tones and highlights...

Still writing paint functions...

I'm estimating texel density for the painted texture and bumping paint resolution to 2048 for crispness. Now I'm working out leg geometry with hip positions and limb segment proportions for each side.

Writing leg chain code...

Adding the hock spur spike, ankle twine wraps, then moving on to arm coordinates and finger loops before tackling the head and decorations, including hanging hair strands behind the skull.

I'm checking whether the hair would clip through the torso given the neck's forward lean -- the straight vertical hang from the back of the skull seems to float past the shoulders rather than resting against them, so I should angle the hair strands backward along a lean direction to follow the neck's curve more naturally.

Working through the card orientation geometry, the plane spans the width and lean directions, with the normal perpendicular to the down-back lean—since cards are double-sided it'll read fine from either viewpoint. Now I'm thinking about adding fur texture to the cape, with frames hanging down.

Setting up the glow helper and material cache...

Good, glow runs right after creation so the material exists by then. Now I'm sketching a wrap helper that builds a ring frame and sweeps a catmull curve through it with a given thickness and color, and I need to figure out how to type the color parameter loosely enough to accept both strings and paint objects.

Writing rib loop code...

Adding the ember wound at the torso's center, embedding a crater cylinder and a glowing sphere offset slightly outward along the normal, and working out how the embed fraction sinks the sphere's center relative to its own diameter.

I'll go with base-at-surface placement: for sphere r=.062 with embed 0.3, sunk by 0.037 gives a bulge of 0.087, which checks out. I'm also confirming rib placement near 166/174 degrees with the heart centered at 180 between ribs, and verifying torso ribs span the .40-.82 range correctly, plus working through how the sternum sweep line slices along the torso surface at that clock angle.

The sternum would pass straight through the heart sphere if I slice it continuously, so instead I'm splitting it into two separate pieces that avoid the heart region entirely, slicing around 0.42-0.60 and 0.70-0.86. I'm assigning SKIN paint to the torso and BONEP paint to the ribs, and writing the BONEP paint function that mixes tan and dark bone tones using layered noise plus a shading term based on surface normal. Now I'm starting on the skull paint function.

Still writing paint shader...

Now I'm pivoting to ear points using SKIN, then designing forearm card ribbons and belt-hanging charms, using hex card shapes with a 180-degree lean for the dangling pieces.

Writing belt rag code...

I'm checking that card orientation along the flow axis makes sense at the sides of the hips, since cards facing front-back would look edge-on there rather than fully visible.

Now I'm setting up a shoulder loop for cape strips, defining the plane around a specific torso point and filtering frames by their z-position to isolate the back portion.

I'm orienting those strips to hang downward with a slight backward lean so they drape naturally along the torso's back slope, varying their sizes for a more organic look. I'm also considering adding a diagonal bandolier sash across the chest using a rough path of points looped around the torso.

Now I'm scattering fur card elements on the shoulders, positioned only above a certain height, with small sizes and some lean, bend, and spin variation for a shaggy texture. I'm also planning a lighter frost scatter layer on the shoulders using similar scatter parameters.

Setting up the arm structure next, defining shoulder, elbow, and wrist anchor points mirrored for left and right sides, and using a catmull-rom chain through those three points to get a naturally curved limb shape.

Still writing arm radii...

Still writing finger chains...
